title: Ὁ Γέρων τῆς Θαλάσσης
titleEn: The Old Man of the Sea — Odyssey 4.332–434
part: The Old Man of the Sea (4.332–434)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Menelaus answers Telemachus's plea by telling how the gods becalmed him on the island of Pharos off Egypt, and how the sea-nymph Eidothea, taking pity on him, taught him to ambush her shape-shifting father Proteus, the Old Man of the Sea, and hold him fast until he answered truly; Menelaus then tells how, at dawn among the seals, he and three companions did just that.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.tr: ton de meg’ ochthēsas prosephē xanthos Menelaos·
sentences.l: Him then, greatly vexed, addressed fair-haired Menelaus:
sentences.i: Then, greatly troubled, fair-haired Menelaus said to him:
sentences.n: This whole line repeats 4.30 (as already published in odyssey-014, where it is the unit at Murray line 30), and keeps the same English. ξανθὸς Μενέλαος, ‘fair-haired Menelaus’, is the house rendering used throughout for his standing epithet.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, ἦ μάλα δὴ κρατερόφρονος ἀνδρὸς ἐν εὐνῇ
ἤθελον εὐνηθῆναι ἀνάλκιδες αὐτοὶ ἐόντες.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi, ē mala dē kraterophronos andros en eunēi
ēthelon eunēthēnai analkides autoi eontes.
sentences.l:
“Ah! surely indeed in the bed of a strong-minded man
they wished to lie, themselves being men without might.
sentences.i: “Ah, they surely wished to lie in the bed of a mighty-minded man, weaklings that they themselves are!
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is the fixed exclamation ‘Ah!’. κρατερόφρων, ‘strong-minded, stout of heart’, is a new compound of κρατερός and φρήν, distinct from the -φρων epithets already fixed for Odysseus; it describes Odysseus himself, whose bed and wife the suitors covet. εὐνηθῆναι is an aorist passive infinitive of εὐνάω ‘lie in bed’, used here in a middle sense; ἀνάλκιδες, ‘without might, strengthless’ (ἀ- + ἀλκή), is a predicate adjective on the implied subject, the suitors. This is the first unit of Menelaus's own speech; the reply-formula of the line before it is narration only.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὁπότ’ ἐν ξυλόχῳ ἔλαφος κρατεροῖο λέοντος
νεβροὺς κοιμήσασα νεηγενέας γαλαθηνοὺς
κνημοὺς ἐξερέῃσι καὶ ἄγκεα ποιήεντα
βοσκομένη,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hopot’ en xylochōi elaphos krateroio leontos
nebrous koimēsasa neēgeneas galathēnous
knēmous exereēisi kai ankea poiēenta
boskomenē,
sentences.l:
And as when, in the lair of a mighty lion, a hind,
her newborn, milk-fed fawns having lulled to rest,
ranges the wooded slopes and grassy glens,
grazing,
sentences.i: And as when a hind, having lulled her newborn, milk-fed fawns to rest in the lair of a mighty lion, ranges the wooded slopes and grassy glens as she grazes,
sentences.n: This four-line simile runs to 340; the true stop does not come until the end of line 340, six lines from its start, so the cut here falls at the strongest comma instead, as the rules require. ξύλοχος is a thicket or lair; νεηγενής ‘newborn’ and γαλαθηνός ‘milk-fed, suckling’ are epic compound adjectives, not verb forms, so no augment/no-augment claim applies to them. ἐξερέῃσι is an epic subjunctive in -ῃσι (ἐξερέομαι ‘search out, range over’) used generalizing with ὁπότε in a vivid present-tense simile, needing no ἄν/κε. κνημούς, ‘mountain slopes, spurs’, and ἄγκεα ποιήεντα, ‘grassy glens’, are the hind's grazing-grounds. This whole simile, new in this part, is recorded in new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἔπειτα ἑὴν εἰσήλυθεν εὐνήν,
ἀμφοτέροισι δὲ τοῖσιν ἀεικέα πότμον ἐφῆκεν,
ὣς Ὀδυσεὺς κείνοισιν ἀεικέα πότμον ἐφήσει.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ epeita heēn eisēlythen eunēn,
amphoteroisi de toisin aeikea potmon ephēken,
hōs Odyseus keinoisin aeikea potmon ephēsei.
sentences.i: but the lion then came back to his own lair, and sent an unseemly doom upon them both; so will Odysseus send an unseemly doom upon those men.
sentences.n: εὐνήν, ‘his own lair’, is the same noun used of Odysseus's marriage-bed five lines above (εὐνῇ, 333): the simile's word bridges from the man's bed to the beast's den. ἀεικέα πότμον, ‘an unseemly doom’ (ἀεικής ‘unfitting, shameful’ + πότμος ‘fate, doom’), is repeated verbatim in successive lines (339, 340) as a deliberate refrain and is fixed as a new house rendering. ἐφῆκεν and ἐφήσει are the aorist and future of ἐφίημι, ‘send/let loose upon’.

sentences.t:
αἲ γάρ, Ζεῦ τε πάτερ καὶ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἄπολλον,
τοῖος ἐών, οἷός ποτ’ ἐυκτιμένῃ ἐνὶ Λέσβῳ
ἐξ ἔριδος Φιλομηλεΐδῃ ἐπάλαισεν ἀναστάς,
κὰδ δ’ ἔβαλε κρατερῶς, κεχάροντο δὲ πάντες Ἀχαιοί,
sentences.tr:
ai gar, Zeu te pater kai Athēnaiē kai Apollon,
toios eōn, hoios pot’ eyktimenēi eni Lesbōi
ex eridos Philomēleïdēi epalaisen anastas,
kad d’ ebale kraterōs, kecharonto de pantes Achaioi,
sentences.l:
Would that — Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo —
such as he was, when once in well-built Lesbos,
rising up from a quarrel, he wrestled against Philomeleides,
and threw him down mightily, and all the Achaeans rejoiced —
sentences.i: If only — Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo — Odysseus were such as he was when once, in well-built Lesbos, he rose up from a quarrel and wrestled Philomeleides, and threw him down hard, to the joy of all the Achaeans —
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ with the optative that follows (ὁμιλήσειεν, 345) is a wish, ‘would that’; the whole four-line vocative invocation Ζεῦ τε πάτερ καὶ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἄπολλον is a stock wish-opening likely to recur later in the poem and is fixed here as a new house rendering. ἐυκτιμένῃ echoes the already-fixed ‘well-built’ of ἐυκτίμενον πτολίεθρον (3.4), now applied to an island. Φιλομηλεΐδης is a legendary king of Lesbos known to us only from this wrestling story; κὰδ ἔβαλε is tmesis for κατέβαλε, ‘threw down’; κεχάροντο is a reduplicated aorist of χαίρω, ‘rejoiced’, with no augment. Because the true stop (·, at the end of 345) would otherwise put this unit at five lines, the cut falls instead at the strongest comma, after Ἀχαιοί.

sentences.t: τοῖος ἐὼν μνηστῆρσιν ὁμιλήσειεν Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: toios eōn mnēstērsin homilēseien Odysseus·
sentences.l: being such, may Odysseus come among the suitors;
sentences.i: then, being such a man, Odysseus might come among the suitors!
sentences.n: This line (τοῖος ἐὼν μνηστῆρσιν ὁμιλήσειεν Ὀδυσσεύς) is identical to 3.264 (odyssey-003), where it closed a different sentence about Odysseus's love for Antilochus; here it completes the wish begun at 341, so only its own wording is reused, not the odyssey-003 sentence around it. ὁμιλήσειεν is optative, continuing the wish of αἲ γάρ.

sentences.t: πάντες κ’ ὠκύμοροί τε γενοίατο πικρόγαμοί τε.
sentences.tr: pantes k’ ōkymoroi te genoiato pikrogamoi te.
sentences.l: all of them would become swift-doomed and bitter-wedded.
sentences.i: All of them would meet a swift doom and a bitter marriage.
sentences.n: This line repeats 3.266 (odyssey-003) exactly and is already fixed in the house-renderings table; γενοίατο is a further optative parallel to ὁμιλήσειεν, completing the same wish.

sentences.t:
ταῦτα δ’ ἅ μ’ εἰρωτᾷς καὶ λίσσεαι, οὐκ ἂν ἐγώ γε
ἄλλα παρὲξ εἴποιμι παρακλιδόν, οὐδ’ ἀπατήσω,
ἀλλὰ τὰ μέν μοι ἔειπε γέρων ἅλιος νημερτής,
τῶν οὐδέν τοι ἐγὼ κρύψω ἔπος οὐδ’ ἐπικεύσω.
sentences.tr:
tauta d’ ha m’ eirōtāis kai lisseai, ouk an egō ge
alla parex eipoimi paraklidon, oud’ apatēsō,
alla ta men moi eeipe gerōn halios nēmertēs,
tōn ouden toi egō krypsō epos oud’ epikeusō.
sentences.l:
But these things which you ask me and beg of me, I myself
would not say otherwise, in a roundabout way, nor will I deceive you;
but what the unerring old man of the sea told me,
of that I will hide from you no word, nor keep anything back.
sentences.i: But as for these things you ask and beg of me, I for my part will not speak beside the point, evasively, nor will I deceive you; rather, what the unerring old man of the sea told me — of that I will hide no word from you, nor keep anything back.
sentences.n: εἰρωτᾷς...λίσσεαι echoes λίσσομαι, the verb that opens the last sentence of Telemachus's plea to Menelaus, carried over from the previous part (‘λίσσομαι, εἴ ποτέ ...’, 4.328). οὐκ ἄν...εἴποιμι is a potential optative, ‘I would not say’; παρακλιδόν, ‘aslant, evasively’, is a rare adverb for speaking in a way that swerves from the truth. γέρων ἅλιος νημερτής, ‘the unerring old man of the sea’, is Proteus's standing epithet in this whole episode, recurring at 384 and 401, and is fixed here as a new house rendering. κρύψω and ἐπικεύσω are near-synonym futures doubled for emphasis, ‘hide’ and ‘conceal further’.

sentences.t:
Αἰγύπτῳ μ’ ἔτι δεῦρο θεοὶ μεμαῶτα νέεσθαι
ἔσχον, ἐπεὶ οὔ σφιν ἔρεξα τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας.
sentences.tr:
Aigyptōi m’ eti deuro theoi memaōta neesthai
eschon, epei ou sphin erexa telēessas hekatombas.
sentences.l:
In Egypt me, still eager to come hither,
the gods held back, since to them I had not offered complete hecatombs.
sentences.i: The gods kept me back in Egypt, though I was still eager to come home, because I had not offered them complete hecatombs.
sentences.n: Αἴγυπτος here names the river (or land) of Egypt; νέεσθαι, uncontracted (Attic νεῖσθαι), shares its root with νόστος. τεληέσσας, ‘complete, fulfilling’ (from τέλος), describes hecatombs performed in full and correctly; whether the completeness is ritual or numerical is not certain.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ αἰεὶ βούλοντο θεοὶ μεμνῆσθαι ἐφετμέων.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ aiei boulonto theoi memnēsthai ephetmeōn.
sentences.l: But the gods always wished that men be mindful of their commands.
sentences.i: But the gods always wanted their commands to be kept in mind.
sentences.n: ἐφετμέων, ‘commands, injunctions’, is an epic noun rare outside Homer; μεμνῆσθαι is a perfect infinitive with present force, ‘to be mindful’, its subject (men in general) left unstated.

sentences.t:
νῆσος ἔπειτά τις ἔστι πολυκλύστῳ ἐνὶ πόντῳ
Αἰγύπτου προπάροιθε, Φάρον δέ ἑ κικλήσκουσι,
τόσσον ἄνευθ’ ὅσσον τε πανημερίη γλαφυρὴ νηῦς
ἤνυσεν, ᾗ λιγὺς οὖρος ἐπιπνείῃσιν ὄπισθεν·
sentences.tr:
nēsos epeita tis esti polyklystōi eni pontōi
Aigyptou proparoithe, Pharon de he kiklēskousi,
tosson aneuth’ hosson te panēmeriē glaphyrē nēus
ēnysen, hēi ligys ouros epipneiēisin opisthen·
sentences.l:
There is then a certain island in the much-surging sea,
in front of Egypt, and Pharos they call it,
as far off as a hollow ship accomplishes in a whole day,
for which a shrill fair wind blows from behind;
sentences.i: There is an island out in the surging sea, off the coast of Egypt, called Pharos, as far off as a hollow ship can make in a full day's sailing, when a clear following wind blows behind it;
sentences.n: πολύκλυστος, ‘much-dashed-by-waves’, is built on κλύζω ‘surge, wash over’. γλαφυρὴ νηῦς, ‘hollow ship’, uses the same adjective already fixed for ‘hollow caves’ (1.15). Pharos is named here for the first time in the poem. λιγύς, ‘clear, shrill’, and οὖρος, ‘a fair, favouring wind’, describe ideal sailing conditions.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ λιμὴν ἐύορμος, ὅθεν τ’ ἀπὸ νῆας ἐίσας
ἐς πόντον βάλλουσιν, ἀφυσσάμενοι μέλαν ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr:
en de limēn eyormos, hothen t’ apo nēas eisas
es ponton ballousin, aphyssamenoi melan hydōr.
sentences.l:
and in it is a harbor of good anchorage, from where men launch
their well-balanced ships into the sea, having drawn dark water.
sentences.i: In it there is a harbor with good anchorage, from which men launch their well-balanced ships out to sea, once they have drawn dark water for the voyage.
sentences.n: ἐύορμος, ‘with good anchorage/mooring’, describes the harbor; ἐίσας, ‘well-balanced’ (accusative plural), repeats the already-fixed epithet of νηῦς ἐίση (3.10). ἀφυσσάμενοι μέλαν ὕδωρ describes drawing fresh water aboard before a voyage.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μ’ ἐείκοσιν ἤματ’ ἔχον θεοί, οὐδέ ποτ’ οὖροι
πνείοντες φαίνονθ’ ἁλιαέες, οἵ ῥά τε νηῶν
πομπῆες γίγνονται ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr:
entha m’ eeikosin ēmat’ echon theoi, oude pot’ ouroi
pneiontes phainonth’ haliaees, hoi rha te nēōn
pompēes gignontai ep’ eurea nōta thalassēs.
sentences.l:
There the gods held me twenty days, nor ever did winds
appear blowing, sea-borne ones, which indeed for ships
become escorts over the broad back of the sea.
sentences.i: There the gods kept me for twenty days, and never once did the sea-borne winds appear that serve as escorts for ships over the sea's broad back.
sentences.n: ἐείκοσι has the epic prothetic vowel (Attic εἴκοσι). ἁλιαής, ‘blowing off the sea’, is a rare compound found only here in Homer. ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης, ‘over the broad back of the sea’, pictures the sea's surface as a single broad back to be crossed, though νῶτα is grammatically plural; the phrase is likely to recur and is fixed here as a new house rendering, kept singular in English as the idiom requires.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κεν ἤια πάντα κατέφθιτο καὶ μένε’ ἀνδρῶν,
εἰ μή τίς με θεῶν ὀλοφύρατο καί μ’ ἐσάωσε,
Πρωτέος ἰφθίμου θυγάτηρ ἁλίοιο γέροντος,
Εἰδοθέη·
sentences.tr:
kai ny ken ēia panta katephthito kai mene’ andrōn,
ei mē tis me theōn olophyrato kai m’ esaōse,
Prōteos iphthimou thygatēr halioio gerontos,
Eidotheē·
sentences.l:
And now indeed all our stores would have perished, and the men's strength,
had not one of the gods pitied me and saved me,
the daughter of mighty Proteus, the old man of the sea,
Eidothea;
sentences.i: And by now all our stores, and the men's strength with them, would have been used up, had not one of the gods taken pity on me and saved me — the daughter of mighty Proteus, the old man of the sea, Eidothea —
sentences.n: κε with the aorist κατέφθιτο is a past unreal condition, ‘would have perished’; ἤια, ‘provisions’, is unrelated to ἠώς/ἠοῖ ‘dawn’ despite the similar spelling. ἴφθιμος, ‘stout, mighty’, is a general epithet of strength or rank. Both Proteus and Eidothea are named here for the first time in the poem; her name is withheld to the very end of the sentence, after her father's name and epithet, a normal device of suspense in the verse. This whole noun-phrase, ‘the daughter of mighty Proteus, the old man of the sea’, is fixed as a new house rendering, kept distinct from the fuller formula γέρων ἅλιος νημερτής fixed at 349, since νημερτής ‘unerring’ is absent here.

sentences.t: τῇ γάρ ῥα μάλιστά γε θυμὸν ὄρινα.
sentences.tr: tēi gar rha malista ge thymon orina.
sentences.l: for her heart, indeed, above all others, I moved.
sentences.i: for I moved her heart more than any other's.
sentences.n: ὄρινα is an unaugmented first-person aorist of ὀρίνω, ‘stir, move (the heart)’; the dative τῇ singles out Eidothea as the one specially moved to pity Menelaus, as against the other gods who might have helped him but did not.

sentences.t: ἥ μ’ οἴῳ ἔρροντι συνήντετο νόσφιν ἑταίρων·
sentences.tr: hē m’ oiōi erronti synēnteto nosphin hetairōn·
sentences.l: She met with me, alone, wandering, apart from my companions;
sentences.i: She came upon me as I wandered alone, away from my companions;
sentences.n: μ’ here stands for the dative μοι (elided before a vowel, not the accusative με), agreeing with the dative participle ἔρροντι, since συναντάω regularly takes the dative of the person met. ἔρρω, ‘wander, roam’ (elsewhere often ‘go wretchedly, go to ruin’), here describes Menelaus's aimless, unhappy roaming on the shore.

sentences.t:
αἰεὶ γὰρ περὶ νῆσον ἀλώμενοι ἰχθυάασκον
γναμπτοῖς ἀγκίστροισιν, ἔτειρε δὲ γαστέρα λιμός.
sentences.tr:
aiei gar peri nēson alōmenoi ichthyaaskon
gnamptois ankistroisin, eteire de gastera limos.
sentences.l:
for always, roaming about the island, we kept fishing
with bent hooks, and hunger wore away our bellies.
sentences.i: for we kept roaming round the island, always fishing with bent hooks, while hunger wore away at our bellies.
sentences.n: ἰχθυάασκον is an iterative imperfect (the -ασκ- suffix marking repeated, habitual action) of the denominative verb ἰχθυάω ‘fish’, built on ἰχθύς. γναμπτοῖς ἀγκίστροισιν, ‘with bent hooks’, is the ordinary Homeric picture of a fish-hook.

sentences.t: ἡ δέ μευ ἄγχι στᾶσα ἔπος φάτο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: hē de meu anchi stasa epos phato phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: And she, having stood near me, spoke a word, and addressed me:
sentences.i: And she came and stood close by me, and spoke, and said:
sentences.n: This is a formula of speech-introduction distinct from the reply-formulas seen so far (name/pronoun + ‘having stood near’ + ‘spoke a word and addressed’); ἔπος φάτο φώνησέν τε doubles two near-synonyms for emphasis, as κρύψω/ἐπικεύσω did at 350. This unit is narration, not itself the start of a speech; the mark belongs to the next unit, where Eidothea's own words begin.

sentences.t:
νήπιός εἰς, ὦ ξεῖνε, λίην τόσον ἠδὲ χαλίφρων,
ἦε ἑκὼν μεθίεις καὶ τέρπεαι ἄλγεα πάσχων;
sentences.tr:
nēpios eis, ō xeine, liēn toson ēde chaliphrōn,
ēe hekōn methieis kai terpeai algea paschōn;
sentences.l:
‘You are foolish, O stranger, so very much, and slack of wit,
or else willingly you slacken, and take pleasure in suffering pains?
sentences.i: ‘You are very foolish indeed, stranger, and slow of wit — or is it that you give up on purpose, and enjoy suffering these pains?
sentences.n: χαλίφρων, ‘slack-minded, foolish’ (χαλάω ‘slacken’ + φρήν), is a rare compound, distinct from all the -φρων epithets already fixed for Odysseus. μεθίημι in the middle can mean ‘relax one's effort, give up’, here set against genuine helplessness. This is the first unit of a speech nested inside Menelaus's own; a single quotation mark is used for it, since his outer speech already carries double quotation marks.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὴ δήθ’ ἐνὶ νήσῳ ἐρύκεαι, οὐδέ τι τέκμωρ
εὑρέμεναι δύνασαι, μινύθει δέ τοι ἦτορ ἑταίρων.
sentences.tr:
hōs dē dēth’ eni nēsōi erykeai, oude ti tekmōr
heuremenai dynasai, minythei de toi ētor hetairōn.
sentences.l:
seeing that for so long now on the island you are held back, nor can you
find any end to it, and the heart of your companions wastes away.’
sentences.i: since you are held so long on this island and can find no way out of it, while the hearts of your companions waste away.’
sentences.n: τέκμωρ, ‘a fixed mark, an end or limit’, is an old noun (cf. τεκμήριον) used here of an escape not being found; εὑρέμεναι is an infinitive in -έμεναι (Attic εὑρεῖν). ἦτορ ἑταίρων, ‘the heart of your companions’, is singular for a plural of persons, a normal Homeric idiom. Eidothea's first speech closes here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autar egō min ameibomenos proseeipon·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: ἔφατ(ο) is the same verb-form used generically for ‘spoke’ whatever the speaker's gender (cf. the fixed ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’); here the subject is Eidothea. ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον is a first-person variant of the reply-formulas already fixed for the third person, built instead with the aorist προσέειπον, ‘I addressed’. This is narration, not the start of a new speech; the mark belongs to the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἐκ μέν τοι ἐρέω, ἥ τις σύ πέρ ἐσσι θεάων,
ὡς ἐγὼ οὔ τι ἑκὼν κατερύκομαι, ἀλλά νυ μέλλω
ἀθανάτους ἀλιτέσθαι, οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν.
sentences.tr:
ek men toi ereō, hē tis sy per essi theaōn,
hōs egō ou ti hekōn katerykomai, alla ny mellō
athanatous alitesthai, hoi ouranon euryn echousin.
sentences.l:
‘I will indeed tell you outright, whoever of the goddesses you are,
that I am held back not at all of my own will, but I must be
offending the immortals, who the wide sky hold.
sentences.i: ‘I will tell you plainly, whoever among the goddesses you are, that I am not held back of my own will, but that I must be offending the immortals who hold the wide sky.
sentences.n: ἐκ...ἐρέω is tmesis for ἐξερέω, ‘declare, speak out’; ἐσσι is the epic 2nd sg. of εἰμί (Attic εἶ). μέλλω with the infinitive here expresses a supposition, ‘I must be, it seems’; ἀλιτέσθαι is from ἀλιταίνω, ‘sin against, transgress against’. οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν, ‘who hold the wide sky’, is the same standing periphrasis for the gods already rendered this way at 1.65–67 (odyssey-001). This is the first unit of Menelaus's own past reply to Eidothea, a speech nested inside his present speech to Telemachus; it takes its own single quotation mark.
sentences.mark: Menelaus recalls his answer to Eidothea

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ πέρ μοι εἰπέ, θεοὶ δέ τε πάντα ἴσασιν,
ὅς τίς μ’ ἀθανάτων πεδάᾳ καὶ ἔδησε κελεύθου,
νόστον θ’, ὡς ἐπὶ πόντον ἐλεύσομαι ἰχθυόεντα.
sentences.tr:
alla sy per moi eipe, theoi de te panta isasin,
hos tis m’ athanatōn pedaāi kai edēse keleuthou,
noston th’, hōs epi ponton eleusomai ichthyoenta.
sentences.l:
But you, for your part, tell me — and the gods know all things —
which of the immortals fetters me and has bound me from my path,
and of my return, how I shall come upon the fish-teeming sea.’
sentences.i: But you at least tell me — since the gods know everything — which of the immortals holds me fettered and has barred my way, and how I am to make my way home across the fish-teeming sea.’
sentences.n: πεδάᾳ is present indicative, uncontracted, of πεδάω ‘fetter’; κελεύθου is a genitive of separation with ἔδησε, ‘has bound me away from my path’. νόστον θ’, ὡς ἐπὶ πόντον ἐλεύσομαι/ἐλεύσεαι ἰχθυόεντα is a fixed formula in this episode (‘and of my/your return, how I/you shall come upon the fish-teeming sea’), recurring as ἐλεύσεαι (2nd sg.) at 390 and 424 once Eidothea addresses Menelaus in turn; it is fixed here as a new house rendering. This closes Menelaus's first recalled reply to Eidothea.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ἡ δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμείβετο δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, hē d’ autik’ ameibeto dia theaōn·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and she at once answered, heavenly-one of goddesses:
sentences.i: So I said, and she, heavenly even among goddesses, answered at once:
sentences.n: ἐφάμην is the imperfect middle of φημί, first person, ‘I was speaking’; δῖα θεάων is the fixed epithet already used of Calypso in Book 1, applied here to Eidothea.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι, ξεῖνε, μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως ἀγορεύσω.
sentences.tr: toigar egō toi, xeine, mal’ atrekeōs agoreusō.
sentences.l: “Well then, I will tell you, stranger, very exactly.
sentences.i: “Then I will tell you, stranger, quite exactly.
sentences.n: This whole line is a fixed formula already used elsewhere in the poem (3.214, spoken there by Telemachus); its wording is reused byte for byte, including the published double quotation mark, though this speech is itself nested inside Menelaus's own (the convention that a repeated line takes the identical shipped English holds even across a difference in nesting depth, so a single mark is not substituted here).

sentences.t:
πωλεῖταί τις δεῦρο γέρων ἅλιος νημερτὴς
ἀθάνατος Πρωτεὺς Αἰγύπτιος, ὅς τε θαλάσσης
πάσης βένθεα οἶδε, Ποσειδάωνος ὑποδμώς·
sentences.tr:
pōleitai tis deuro gerōn halios nēmertēs
athanatos Prōteus Aigyptios, hos te thalassēs
pasēs benthea oide, Poseidaōnos hypodmōs·
sentences.i: There is one who comes here regularly, the unerring old man of the sea, immortal Proteus of Egypt, who knows the depths of the whole sea, a servant of Poseidon;
sentences.n: πωλεῖται is present with iterative force, ‘he comes and goes regularly’. γέρων ἅλιος νημερτής recurs here for the second time (cf. 349). ὅς τε θαλάσσης πάσης βένθεα οἶδε repeats, aside from the metrically movable ν of οἶδε, the very formula already fixed for Atlas at 1.52–53 (odyssey-001, ‘who of the sea entire the depths knows’), so the same English is kept for it here. ὑποδμώς, ‘an underling, a subject slave’, is a rare and rather startling word to apply to a god, marking Proteus's subordinate rank beneath Poseidon; ἀθάνατος Πρωτεὺς Αἰγύπτιος is fixed here as a new house rendering.

sentences.t: τὸν δέ τ’ ἐμόν φασιν πατέρ’ ἔμμεναι ἠδὲ τεκέσθαι.
sentences.tr: ton de t’ emon phasin pater’ emmenai ēde tekesthai.
sentences.l: And him they say to be my father, and to have begotten me.
sentences.i: They say that he is my father, and that he begot me.
sentences.n: ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί (= Attic εἶναι); τεκέσθαι, the aorist middle infinitive of τίκτω, is regularly used of the father's part in begetting a child (the active is used of the mother's bearing).

sentences.t:
τόν γ’ εἴ πως σὺ δύναιο λοχησάμενος λελαβέσθαι,
ὅς κέν τοι εἴπῃσιν ὁδὸν καὶ μέτρα κελεύθου
νόστον θ’, ὡς ἐπὶ πόντον ἐλεύσεαι ἰχθυόεντα.
sentences.tr:
ton g’ ei pōs sy dynaio lochēsamenos lelabesthai,
hos ken toi eipēisin hodon kai metra keleuthou
noston th’, hōs epi ponton eleuseai ichthyoenta.
sentences.l:
Him, if somehow you could, having lain in ambush, catch and hold,
who would tell you the way and the measures of your path,
and of your return, how you shall come upon the fish-teeming sea.
sentences.i: If somehow you could lie in ambush and catch hold of him, he would tell you the way and the distances of your journey, and how you are to make your way home across the fish-teeming sea.
sentences.n: λοχησάμενος...λελαβέσθαι, ‘having lain in ambush, to catch hold of’, pairs an aorist participle with a perfect middle infinitive of λαμβάνω, stressing a firm, lasting grip; μέτρα κελεύθου, ‘the measures of the way’, means the distances and stages of the route. The fixed formula νόστον θ’, ὡς ἐπὶ πόντον ἐλεύσεαι ἰχθυόεντα recurs here in the second person (cf. ἐλεύσομαι, first person, at 381).

sentences.t:
καὶ δέ κέ τοι εἴπῃσι, διοτρεφές, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα,
ὅττι τοι ἐν μεγάροισι κακόν τ’ ἀγαθόν τε τέτυκται
οἰχομένοιο σέθεν δολιχὴν ὁδὸν ἀργαλέην τε.
sentences.tr:
kai de ke toi eipēisi, diotrephes, ai k’ ethelēistha,
hotti toi en megaroisi kakon t’ agathon te tetyktai
oichomenoio sethen dolichēn hodon argaleēn te.
sentences.l:
And he would tell you also, Zeus-nurtured one, if you should wish it,
whatever, good and bad, has come to pass in your halls
while you have been gone this long and grievous road.”
sentences.i: And he would tell you too, Zeus-nurtured, if you wished it, whatever, good or bad, has happened in your household while you have been gone on this long and grievous journey.”
sentences.n: διοτρεφές reuses the already-fixed ‘Zeus-nurtured’ (cf. 4.156). ἐθέλῃσθα is a 2nd sg. subjunctive with the epic ending -σθα. τέτυκται is a perfect passive of τεύχω, ‘has been made/has come to pass’; οἰχομένοιο σέθεν is a genitive absolute, ‘you being away’, with δολιχὴν ὁδὸν ἀργαλέην τε describing that absence; ἀργαλέος is kept to the same rendering, ‘grievous’, already fixed for μνηστὺς ἀργαλέη. Eidothea's second speech closes here, with a double rather than single closing mark to pair with its opening unit's byte-for-byte reused “ at 383 (forced by the repeated-line rule; see that unit's note).

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autar egō min ameibomenos proseeipon·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: This line repeats 4.375 word for word within this same part, and keeps the same English, as the convention for a repeated line requires.

sentences.t:
αὐτὴ νῦν φράζευ σὺ λόχον θείοιο γέροντος,
μή πώς με προϊδὼν ἠὲ προδαεὶς ἀλέηται·
sentences.tr:
autē nyn phrazeu sy lochon theioio gerontos,
mē pōs me proïdōn ēe prodaeis aleētai·
sentences.l:
‘You yourself now devise the ambush for the divine old man,
lest somehow, having foreseen or learned of it beforehand, he escape me;
sentences.i: ‘Plan the ambush for the divine old man yourself, in case he somehow sees it coming or learns of it beforehand and gets away from me;
sentences.n: φράζευ is a present middle imperative, 2nd sg. in -ευ (epic for -ου). θείοιο is a genitive in -οιο, the epithet θεῖος ‘divine’ now applied to Proteus, kept distinct from the fuller γέρων ἅλιος νημερτής fixed at 349, since Homer uses a different adjective here. προδαείς is built on the same root δαῆναι ‘learn’ that underlies the disputed epithet δαΐφρων (cf. odyssey-001, 1.48). This is the first unit of Menelaus's second recalled reply to Eidothea; it takes its own single quotation mark.
sentences.mark: Menelaus recalls his second answer to Eidothea

sentences.t: ἀργαλέος γάρ τ’ ἐστὶ θεὸς βροτῷ ἀνδρὶ δαμῆναι.
sentences.tr: argaleos gar t’ esti theos brotōi andri damēnai.
sentences.l: for a god is hard for a mortal man to subdue.’
sentences.i: for it is hard for a mortal man to master a god.’
sentences.n: δαμῆναι, aorist passive infinitive of δαμάζω ‘subdue, tame’, is an epexegetic infinitive explaining in what respect a god is ἀργαλέος, ‘hard, grievous’ (the same adjective already fixed as ‘grievous’ for μνηστὺς ἀργαλέη). Menelaus's second recalled reply closes here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ἡ δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμείβετο δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, hē d’ autik’ ameibeto dia theaōn·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and she at once answered, heavenly-one of goddesses:
sentences.i: So I said, and she, heavenly even among goddesses, answered at once:
sentences.n: This line repeats 4.382 word for word within this same part, and keeps the same English. ἀμείβετο is the augmented imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer, reply’ (contrast the unaugmented ἐφάμην beside it, from φημί); δῖα θεάων, ‘heavenly-one of goddesses’, is the house epithet already fixed for Calypso in Book 1, applied to Eidothea at 382 and repeated here unchanged.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι, ξεῖνε, μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως ἀγορεύσω.
sentences.tr: toigar egō toi, xeine, mal’ atrekeōs agoreusō.
sentences.l: “Well then, I will tell you, stranger, very exactly.
sentences.i: “Then I will tell you, stranger, quite exactly.
sentences.n: This is the same fixed formula as 383 (and 3.214), repeated a third time within this part and once more elsewhere in the poem; the same wording, including the published double quotation mark, is kept byte for byte as the shipped-line rule requires, opening Eidothea's third and longest speech (itself nested inside Menelaus's), which now runs to the end of the part.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠέλιος μέσον οὐρανὸν ἀμφιβεβήκῃ,
τῆμος ἄρ’ ἐξ ἁλὸς εἶσι γέρων ἅλιος νημερτὴς
πνοιῇ ὕπο Ζεφύροιο μελαίνῃ φρικὶ καλυφθείς,
ἐκ δ’ ἐλθὼν κοιμᾶται ὑπὸ σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσιν·
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ēelios meson ouranon amphibebēkēi,
tēmos ar’ ex halos eisi gerōn halios nēmertēs
pnoiēi hypo Zephyroio melainēi phriki kalyphtheis,
ek d’ elthōn koimatai hypo spessi glaphyroisin·
sentences.l:
And when the sun has strode to mid-heaven,
then indeed out of the sea comes the unerring old man of the sea,
covered by a dark ripple, under the breath of the West Wind,
and coming forth, he lies down to rest beneath the hollow caves;
sentences.i: When the sun has climbed to the middle of the sky, then the unerring old man of the sea comes up out of the water, hidden under a dark ripple raised by the breath of the West Wind, and comes ashore to sleep in the hollow caves;
sentences.n: ἀμφιβεβήκῃ is a perfect subjunctive of ἀμφιβαίνω, ‘stride astride, bestride’, vivid for the sun's reaching the zenith. εἶσι is the present of εἶμι used with future/habitual force, ‘comes, will come’. γέρων ἅλιος νημερτής recurs a third time here (cf. 349, 384). μελαίνῃ φρικί, ‘with a dark ripple’, pictures the sea's surface rippling as the West Wind blows, veiling Proteus as he rises. σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσιν reuses the fixed rendering ‘hollow caves’ (cf. 1.15).

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ μιν φῶκαι νέποδες καλῆς ἁλοσύδνης
ἁθρόαι εὕδουσιν, πολιῆς ἁλὸς ἐξαναδῦσαι,
πικρὸν ἀποπνείουσαι ἁλὸς πολυβενθέος ὀδμήν.
sentences.tr:
amphi de min phōkai nepodes kalēs halosydnēs
hathroai heudousin, poliēs halos exanadysai,
pikron apopneiousai halos polybentheos odmēn.
sentences.l:
And around him seals, the offspring of fair Halosydne,
sleep all together, having risen up out of the grey sea,
breathing out the bitter smell of the deep-fathomed sea.
sentences.i: And around him seals, the children of fair Halosydne, lie sleeping in a huddled mass, risen up out of the grey sea, breathing out the bitter smell of the deep sea.
sentences.n: νέποδες, ‘offspring, brood’, is a rare and puzzling word used only of these seals in Homer; its formation is disputed. ἁλοσύδνη is an epithet-name for a sea-goddess, usually identified with Amphitrite, whose exact meaning is uncertain; seals are fancifully called her children, and the name is kept as a proper name rather than translated as a common noun. πολιὴ ἅλς reuses the fixed ‘grey sea’; πολυβενθής, ‘very deep, many-fathomed’, is a new compound built on βένθος ‘depth’ (cf. βένθεα, 386). νέποδες and ἁλοσύδνη are both fixed here as new house renderings.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα σ’ ἐγὼν ἀγαγοῦσα ἅμ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφιν
εὐνάσω ἑξείης·
sentences.tr:
entha s’ egōn agagousa ham’ ēoi phainomenēphin
eunasō hexeiēs·
sentences.l:
There I, having led you, together with Dawn as she appears,
will lay you down in a row;
sentences.i: There, at the moment when Dawn appears, I will lead you there and lay you down in a row;
sentences.n: φαινομένηφιν carries the rare instrumental/locative suffix -φι(ν), elsewhere confined to nouns, here attached to a participle — a very unusual formation (Monro discusses the type). ἑξείης, ‘in a row, in succession’, describes how Menelaus and his three chosen men are to be laid out among the seals.

sentences.t:
σὺ δ’ ἐὺ κρίνασθαι ἑταίρους
τρεῖς, οἵ τοι παρὰ νηυσὶν ἐυσσέλμοισιν ἄριστοι.
sentences.tr:
sy d’ ey krinasthai hetairous
treis, hoi toi para nēusin eysselmoisin aristoi.
sentences.l:
but you, choose well three companions,
who beside your well-benched ships are best.
sentences.i: and you must choose well three companions, the best you have beside your well-benched ships.
sentences.n: κρίνασθαι, an aorist middle infinitive, functions here as an imperative, ‘you are to choose’, a common Homeric use of the infinitive (cf. ἔχειν and ἀλύξαι below, 415–416). ἐύσσελμος, ‘well-benched’ (σέλμα ‘rowing-bench, deck-beam’), is a new ship-epithet, kept apart from the already-fixed νηῦς ἐίση, θοὴ νηῦς μέλαινα and κοίλη νηῦς μέλαινα, and fixed here as a new house rendering.

sentences.t: πάντα δέ τοι ἐρέω ὀλοφώια τοῖο γέροντος.
sentences.tr: panta de toi ereō olophōia toio gerontos.
sentences.l: And I will tell you all the baneful wiles of that old man.
sentences.i: And I will tell you all the old man's baneful tricks.
sentences.n: ὀλοφώιος, ‘baneful, harmful, deceitful’, is used substantively here, ‘his baneful arts’; its precise formation is disputed, though some connect it with ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’. τοῖο γέροντος, ‘that old man’, is a plain back-reference to Proteus, distinct from the fuller formula γέρων ἅλιος νημερτής used when he is introduced afresh; ὀλοφώια is fixed here as a new house rendering.

sentences.t: φώκας μέν τοι πρῶτον ἀριθμήσει καὶ ἔπεισιν·
sentences.tr: phōkas men toi prōton arithmēsei kai epeisin·
sentences.l: The seals, first, he will count for you, and go among them;
sentences.i: First he will count the seals and go among them;
sentences.n: ἔπεισιν is present of ἔπειμι ‘go over, inspect’, used with future sense alongside the future ἀριθμήσει, describing Proteus's habitual routine of inspecting his herd of seals.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν πάσας πεμπάσσεται ἠδὲ ἴδηται,
λέξεται ἐν μέσσῃσι νομεὺς ὣς πώεσι μήλων.
sentences.tr:
autar epēn pasas pempassetai ēde idētai,
lexetai en messēisi nomeus hōs pōesi mēlōn.
sentences.l:
But when he has counted them all by fives, and looked them over,
he will lie down among them, like a shepherd among flocks of sheep.
sentences.i: But once he has counted them all off and looked them over, he will lie down among them, like a shepherd among his flocks.
sentences.n: πεμπάζομαι, ‘count by fives’ (built on πέμπε, the old form of πέντε ‘five’), reflects an old finger-counting method. λέξεται is from a separate verb λέχομαι/λέγω ‘lie down to rest’, unrelated to λέγω ‘say, gather’.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐπὴν δὴ πρῶτα κατευνηθέντα ἴδησθε,
καὶ τότ’ ἔπειθ’ ὑμῖν μελέτω κάρτος τε βίη τε,
αὖθι δ’ ἔχειν μεμαῶτα καὶ ἐσσύμενόν περ ἀλύξαι.
sentences.tr:
ton men epēn dē prōta kateunēthenta idēsthe,
kai tot’ epeith’ hymin meletō kartos te biē te,
authi d’ echein memaōta kai essymenon per alyxai.
sentences.l:
But when you first see him laid down to rest,
then after that let your care be strength and force,
and hold him there on the spot, eager though he be, and straining hard to escape.
sentences.i: As soon as you see him lying down to sleep, then let your whole care be strength and force, and hold him fast on the spot, eager as he will be, and straining hard, to get away.
sentences.n: κατευνηθέντα is an aorist passive participle of κατευνάω, ‘lull, lay to rest’; μελέτω is a 3rd-person imperative of μέλω, ‘be a matter of concern’; ἔχειν here (and ἀλύξαι below) is an infinitive used as an imperative, a regular Homeric idiom for commands. κάρτος and βίη, ‘might’ and ‘force’, are near-synonyms doubled for emphasis, as κρύψω/ἐπικεύσω were at 350.

sentences.t:
πάντα δὲ γιγνόμενος πειρήσεται, ὅσσ’ ἐπὶ γαῖαν
ἑρπετὰ γίγνονται, καὶ ὕδωρ καὶ θεσπιδαὲς πῦρ·
sentences.tr:
panta de gignomenos peirēsetai, hoss’ epi gaian
herpeta gignontai, kai hydōr kai thespidaes pyr·
sentences.l:
And becoming all things, he will make trial of you, as many creeping things
as come to be upon the earth, and water, and wondrous-blazing fire;
sentences.i: He will try you by turning into every shape — every creature that lives on the earth, and water, and wondrous-blazing fire;
sentences.n: γιγνόμενος...πειρήσεται describes Proteus's shape-shifting test of his captors' resolve; ἑρπετόν, literally ‘a creeping thing’, is used broadly here for any living creature, not narrowly for reptiles. θεσπιδαής, ‘wondrously blazing’ (θέσπις + δαίω ‘burn’), is a striking compound applied to fire as one of the god's transformations, and is fixed here as a new house rendering.

sentences.t: ὑμεῖς δ’ ἀστεμφέως ἐχέμεν μᾶλλόν τε πιέζειν.
sentences.tr: hymeis d’ astempheōs echemen mallon te piezein.
sentences.l: But you, unflinchingly, hold on, and press all the harder.
sentences.i: But you must hold on unflinchingly, and grip him all the harder.
sentences.n: ἐχέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν (Attic ἔχειν), again used as an imperative; ἀστεμφέως, ‘unyieldingly, without flinching’, and πιέζω, ‘press, squeeze hard’, both stress the physical grip needed to hold the shape-shifting god.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε κεν δή σ’ αὐτὸς ἀνείρηται ἐπέεσσι,
τοῖος ἐὼν οἷόν κε κατευνηθέντα ἴδησθε,
καὶ τότε δὴ σχέσθαι τε βίης λῦσαί τε γέροντα,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote ken dē s’ autos aneirētai epeessi,
toios eōn hoion ke kateunēthenta idēsthe,
kai tote dē schesthai te biēs lysai te geronta,
sentences.l:
But when he himself questions you with words,
being such as you saw him when he lay down to rest,
then indeed hold back from force, and release the old man,
sentences.i: But when he himself questions you with words, still looking just as he did when you saw him lie down, then you must hold back your force and let the old man go,
sentences.n: ἀνείρηται is an aorist subjunctive of ἀνείρομαι, ‘ask, inquire’. οἷόν κε ‘such as ever’ generalizes with κε the comparison to how Menelaus saw Proteus lie down at 414. σχέσθαι, from ἔχω, here means ‘restrain oneself, hold back’ with the genitive βίης, marking the moment the men must release their grip once Proteus resumes speaking in his own true shape. Because the true stop (at the end of 424) would otherwise put this unit at five lines, the cut falls instead at the comma after γέροντα.

sentences.t:
ἥρως, εἴρεσθαι δέ, θεῶν ὅς τίς σε χαλέπτει,
νόστον θ’, ὡς ἐπὶ πόντον ἐλεύσεαι ἰχθυόεντα.
sentences.tr:
hērōs, eiresthai de, theōn hos tis se chaleptei,
noston th’, hōs epi ponton eleuseai ichthyoenta.
sentences.l:
hero, and ask him which of the gods afflicts you,
and of your return, how you shall come upon the fish-teeming sea.’
sentences.i: and ask him — hero that you are — which of the gods is troubling you, and how you are to make your way home across the fish-teeming sea.’
sentences.n: ἥρως, inserted as a vocative in mid-sentence, is a form of direct address to Menelaus, distinct from its use elsewhere in the poem as a narrative title (‘the hero’). χαλέπτει, ‘be harsh to, afflict’, is built on the adjective χαλεπός. The fixed formula νόστον...ἐλεύσεαι ἰχθυόεντα closes the line a third time in this part (cf. 381, 390). This closes Eidothea's third and final speech in this part, and with it the whole three-level nesting of quoted speech; Menelaus's own narration to Telemachus, opened at 333, continues on beyond this point unclosed.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ὑπὸ πόντον ἐδύσετο κυμαίνοντα.
sentences.tr: hōs eipous’ hypo ponton edyseto kymainonta.
sentences.l: So having spoken, she plunged beneath the billowing sea.
sentences.i: With these words she sank beneath the surging sea.
sentences.n: εἰποῦσ’ is the aorist participle of εἶπον, agreeing with the feminine subject, Eidothea; κυμαίνοντα, ‘billowing, surging’ (from κῦμα ‘wave’), describes the sea's swell as she disappears into it. This is plain narration, returning fully to Menelaus's own ongoing account; no quotation mark is needed, since the nested speech already closed at the end of the unit before.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐπὶ νῆας, ὅθ’ ἕστασαν ἐν ψαμάθοισιν,
ἤια·
sentences.tr:
autar egōn epi nēas, hoth’ hestasan en psamathoisin,
ēia·
sentences.l:
But I to the ships, where they stood upon the sands,
was going;
sentences.i: But I made my way to the ships, where they stood upon the sands;
sentences.n: ἕστασαν is a pluperfect-form of ἵστημι with imperfect sense, ‘had stood, stood’; ἤια is the imperfect of εἶμι, ‘I was going, I went’ — a different verb from the uncontracted νέεσθαι at 351, which is from νέομαι and shares its root with νόστος instead, though the two verbs overlap in meaning.

sentences.t: πολλὰ δέ μοι κραδίη πόρφυρε κιόντι.
sentences.tr: polla de moi kradiē porphyre kionti.
sentences.l: and much did my heart churn within me, as I went.
sentences.i: and my heart was in turmoil as I went.
sentences.n: πορφύρω, properly used of the sea heaving and darkening (cf. the adjective πορφύρεος ‘purple’, already fixed at 4.115/154), is applied here metaphorically to a troubled heart; κιόντι is the present participle of κίω, ‘go, walk’, agreeing with the dative μοι.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἐπὶ νῆα κατήλυθον ἠδὲ θάλασσαν,
δόρπον θ’ ὁπλισάμεσθ’, ἐπί τ’ ἤλυθεν ἀμβροσίη νύξ·
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ epi nēa katēlython ēde thalassan,
dorpon th’ hoplisamesth’, epi t’ ēlythen ambrosiē nyx·
sentences.l:
But when then we had come down to the ship and the sea,
we made ready our supper, and upon it came ambrosial night;
sentences.i: But when we had come down to the ship and the sea, we got supper ready, and ambrosial night came on;
sentences.n: κατήλυθον is a root aorist of κατέρχομαι whose ending is identical for 1st singular or plural; in this same line's other occurrence in the poem (4.428, shared with odyssey-008) the subject was 3rd plural, ‘they had come down’, but here, governed by the following 1st-plural ὁπλισάμεσθ(α), it must be 1st person plural, ‘we came down’; the published wording is kept as far as this change of subject allows. ἐπί...ἤλυθεν is tmesis for ἐπῆλθεν, ‘came on, came upon’; ἀμβροσίη νύξ, ‘ambrosial night’, is a standing epic phrase for the divinely restorative dark.

sentences.t: δὴ τότε κοιμήθημεν ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr: dē tote koimēthēmen epi rhēgmini thalassēs.
sentences.l: Then indeed we lay down to sleep upon the surf-line of the sea.
sentences.i: Then we lay down to sleep on the shore where the sea breaks.
sentences.n: ῥηγμίς, ‘the beach where the surf breaks’ (from ῥήγνυμι ‘break’), names the strip of shore right at the waterline, a common resting-place for stranded travellers in the poem.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
καὶ τότε δὴ παρὰ θῖνα θαλάσσης εὐρυπόροιο
ἤια πολλὰ θεοὺς γουνούμενος·
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
kai tote dē para thina thalassēs euryporoio
ēia polla theous gounoumenos·
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, then I went along the shore of the wide-wayed sea, praying earnestly to the gods;
sentences.n: The first line repeats the fixed formula ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς exactly (cf. its other occurrence at 4.431, shared with odyssey-005's opening line) and keeps its established English. εὐρύπορος, ‘with wide paths’, is a new compound (εὐρύς + πόρος ‘way, passage’) built on the same pattern as the already-fixed χθὼν εὐρυόδεια, ‘the wide-wayed earth’, and is fixed here, applied to the sea, as a new house rendering. γουνόομαι, ‘supplicate by the knees’ (γόνυ ‘knee’), is a vivid verb of entreaty describing the physical gesture of Greek supplication even where no one is present to clasp.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἑταίρους
τρεῖς ἄγον, οἷσι μάλιστα πεποίθεα πᾶσαν ἐπ’ ἰθύν.
sentences.tr:
autar hetairous
treis agon, hoisi malista pepoithea pasan ep’ ithyn.
sentences.l:
but my companions,
three, I took along, in whom I trusted most for every undertaking.
sentences.i: and I took along three companions, the ones I trusted most for any undertaking.
sentences.n: πεποίθεα is a pluperfect (with imperfect/perfect force) of πείθω, ‘I had come to trust, I trusted’. ἰθύν, ‘a direct course, an undertaking’, is a distinct noun from the identically spelled adverb ἰθύς ‘straight’. This is the final unit of the part; Menelaus's own frame narration continues beyond it into the next part, so no closing quotation mark is given — the outer quotation mark opened at 333 remains open, to be closed only when a future part resumes and completes his speech, as with the equivalent situations already noted at the ends of odyssey-014 and odyssey-016.
